title: Short Track Race Day: The Complete Competition Checklist for Speed Skaters
thumbnail_text: Short track races are won off the ice

scenes.heading: Short Track Race Day Checklist
scenes.sub: Race week, the night before and the hour before your first heat
scenes.chapter: The race day plan in one line
scenes.narration: This is your full short track race day routine, from race week to the start line. You will get a simple order to follow, a packing list, and a checklist you can copy. Here is the whole plan in one line. Sharpen and settle your blades early in race week. Pack from a written list the night before. Then spend the final hour warming up off the ice and putting your kit on in the same order every time. Get those three things right, and the rest of the day is just racing.

scenes.heading: Why races are won off the ice
scenes.chapter: Why races are won off the ice
bullets: A dull edge washes out on the apex
A loose bolt lets the blade shift
A cold hip cramps in the first corner
Every one is fixable the day before
scenes.narration: Ask experienced skaters where finals are won and lost, and very few point at the ice. They point at the changing room, the bag, and the last hour before the first heat. Short track margins are tiny and the contact is real. A blade that has lost its edge will wash out on the apex, right when you load it hardest. A bolt that backed off by half a turn lets your blade shift under you. A cold hip flexor cramps in the first corner. None of these are talent problems. They are preparation problems, and every one of them is fixable the day before. The skaters who podium again and again treat their gear checks as part of the race.

scenes.heading: Race week: change nothing new
scenes.chapter: Race week: what to leave alone
bullets: Sharpen early, never the night before
Deburr fully, then skate the new edge
Leave bend, rocker and pitch alone
Check every mounting cup bolt
scenes.narration: Race week has one rule. Change nothing that your body has to relearn. Your feet and your balance have spent weeks adapting to your boot, your bend and your rocker. Sharpen early in the week, not the night before. A fresh grind can feel grabby, so skate at least one session on the new edge before you race. Deburr fully so no wire edge drags on the ice. If your setup already feels right, leave it exactly as it is. Write your alignment down, or take a photo of the cup position, so you can return to a known good setup. Then walk through every bolt on your mounting cups. Cups can loosen slowly under side load. If you run adapters or spacers, check they sit square, because a twisted blade feels like a vague, wandering push.

scenes.heading: The three windows of race day
scenes.narration: This timeline splits race day into three windows, each with its own short job list. In race week, you sharpen and deburr early, check every mount bolt, skate the new edge once, and change nothing new. The night before, you pack the full bag, fit your guards and soakers, lay out your race kit, and then sleep instead of tinkering. In the hour before, you warm up off the ice, wipe your edges, fit your gloves, helmet and neck guard, and take your guards off at the line. Nothing is left to chance.

scenes.heading: Pack from a list, not from memory
scenes.chapter: Packing the bag and tool roll
bullets: Boots, hard guards and soft soakers
Race suit, base layer and safety kit
Tool roll with spare bolts and laces
Spare glove tips and a deburr stone
scenes.narration: Packing from memory is how skaters arrive with one glove. Build a written list once and reuse it for every meet. Your bag holds your boots with blades mounted, hard guards for walking around the venue, and soft soakers to pull moisture off the steel. Add your race suit, a spare base layer, your safety kit, a cloth for the edges, tape, water and simple food. Then keep a small tool roll in the bag for good. Put in the driver that fits your cup bolts and two or three spare bolts. Add a spare set of laces, a spare pair of glove tips, and a small diamond deburr stone. All of it fits in a space smaller than a paperback, and it saves meets.

scenes.heading: Pack the bag in layers
scenes.narration: Pack in the order you will use things, so the first thing you need is the first thing your hand finds. The top layer comes out first. That is your helmet, neck guard, undersuit, socks and gloves, because you put your safety kit on first. The middle layer is what you use at the boards: boots with blades, guards, soakers and your race suit. The bottom layer is the one you hope not to need: the tool roll, spare bolts, laces, glove tips and the deburr stone. When you are three heats deep and tired, a bag you can read at a glance saves you from silly mistakes.

scenes.heading: Your last hour before the first heat
bullets: 60 min: jog, hip openers, ankle circles
45 min: three or four short accelerations
30 min: undersuit, suit, neck guard
20 min: boots and helmet
10 min: gloves, wipe edges, guards on
scenes.narration: Aim to arrive ninety minutes before your first heat. That covers a queue at the sharpening bench and a busy changing room. Then follow the same order every time. Sixty minutes out, a light jog, hip openers, ankle circles and a few gentle lunges. Forty five minutes out, three or four accelerations of six to eight seconds with full recovery. Thirty minutes out, undersuit, socks and race suit on, then your neck guard. Twenty minutes out, boots on, laces set, helmet buckled. Ten minutes out, gloves and tips on, wipe the edges dry, and guards on for the walk. Use the official warm up for easy laps and a corner entry or two at pace, then get straight back into warm layers. At the line, guards off, and breathe.

scenes.heading: Keep the edge sharp through the rounds
scenes.narration: A short track edge grips through its two crisp corners. On the left, a sharp square edge bites the ice. On the right, those corners have rounded off, and the blade slides on the apex just when you load it hardest. So protect the edge all day. Wipe the blades with a dry cloth before every heat, because rink ice leaves a film of moisture and grit. Between heats, dry the steel again and slide the soakers on the moment you step off the ice. In a humid rink, standing water starts rust fast. And never walk on bare blades on matting or concrete. One hard step can nick an edge and cost you the meet.

scenes.heading: Wear the full safety kit, every race
scenes.chapter: The safety kit you must wear
scenes.narration: Short track is a contact sport on steel edges, so the safety kit is not optional. This diagram shows how each layer guards a part of the body a blade can reach. A certified helmet. A Level 3 cut resistant neck guard. Gloves with tips. A Level 3 Kevlar undersuit. And Level 4 ankle socks, because the ankle sits low, close to other blades, and spends a long time near the ice in a slide. Add eye protection, shin guards and knee protection. Wear the whole system for every race, never a partial set. Federations and meets publish their own equipment rules, and they change, so read them before you travel. Skaters do get turned away for a missing shin guard.

scenes.heading: When something breaks at the meet
bullets: Loose cup bolt: retighten, check the rest
Snapped lace: replace it, never knot it
Torn glove tip: swap in your spare
Nicked edge: deburr, then check by feel
scenes.narration: Sooner or later, something fails between heats. Decide now what you will do. If a cup bolt has loosened, stop and do not race on it. Bring it back to your usual tension, then check the other three on that boot. If a lace snaps, replace the whole lace. A knot under the tongue makes a pressure point and lets your heel lift. If a glove tip tears, swap in your spare pair. If you nick an edge on matting, take the burr off with your stone and check the edge by feel. If the damage catches a fingernail across the corner, tell your coach before you race on it. Each fix takes a couple of minutes if the parts are in your bag.

scenes.heading: Where food and drink fit
scenes.chapter: Eating and drinking at a meet
scenes.narration: A meet can mean a heat in the morning and a final in the evening, with long gaps between. This timeline shows where food belongs. Eat your main meal before you arrive. After each race, the green window is for real food, small, plain and familiar, taken soon after you come off the ice. The orange stretch before each call is for sips only. Put warm layers on first and food second. Cold air hides thirst, so carry your own bottle and sip steadily all day. Try nothing new on race day, and junior skaters should leave caffeine alone. If you often feel faint, cramp badly or get stomach trouble at meets, speak to a doctor or a registered dietitian.

scenes.heading: Change nothing your body has to relearn
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea to remember. In race week, change nothing your body has to relearn. Sharpen early, pack from a written list, warm up in the same order every time, and wear the full safety kit for every race. Get the preparation right and race day becomes calm. Your edges bite, your kit is on, and all that is left is the racing. The full guide, with the complete checklist and answers to common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
